name: Post-Quantum Crypto Exists
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: The Replacement Was Already Built
lesson.summary: Cryptographers began building quantum resistant algorithms on entirely different mathematical foundations decades before large scale quantum computers existed, so the field was not caught flat footed by the threat Public Key Encryption Basics describes.
lesson.body:
One of the least reported facts in quantum computing coverage is also one of the most reassuring: the cryptography community did not wait around for a quantum computer capable of breaking RSA to show up before starting work on a replacement. Serious research into what is now called post-quantum cryptography, encryption designed to stay secure even against an attacker with a large scale quantum computer, dates back decades, well before quantum hardware existed at meaningful scale, because Shor's algorithm made the eventual threat clear as early as 1994. Coverage of quantum computing risk often implies cryptographers are scrambling to catch up. In reality, a mature body of defensive work was built quietly, over many years, ahead of the threat, not in response to it.

Recall from Public Key Encryption Basics that systems like RSA and elliptic curve cryptography are secure specifically because they rely on mathematical problems, factoring and discrete logarithms, that are hard for classical computers but, per Shor's algorithm, not hard for a sufficiently powerful quantum one. Post-quantum cryptography sidesteps this weakness by building encryption on entirely different mathematical problems, ones nobody, including quantum researchers, currently knows how to solve efficiently even with a quantum computer. Several distinct families have been studied for years: lattice based problems, involving specific points in high dimensional geometric structures, hash based problems, which build on the well studied security of cryptographic hash functions, and others including code based and multivariate polynomial approaches.

It is important to be precise about what "quantum resistant" means, because it is a more modest claim than "quantum proof." These algorithms are believed resistant to attack by both classical and quantum computers based on extensive analysis and years of attempted attacks by the cryptographic research community, the same adversarial scrutiny that gives cryptographers confidence in systems like RSA today. Belief built on sustained, unsuccessful attack attempts by expert cryptanalysts is genuinely the best confidence cryptography ever offers, since no encryption scheme has ever been mathematically proven unbreakable in an absolute sense. This is normal for the field, not unique to post-quantum approaches.

The existence of mature, well studied alternatives changes the emotional register of the encryption threat discussed earlier. If no defense existed and a working solution had to be invented only after a capable quantum computer appeared, the Harvest Now, Decrypt Later threat covered next would be a genuine crisis with no clear resolution. Instead, the practical challenge is closer to a large, well understood engineering project: migrating existing systems, from browsers to banking to government communications, onto already designed, already analyzed replacement algorithms. That is substantial given how much infrastructure runs on older cryptography, but it is a far more solvable problem than inventing new mathematics under time pressure.

This distinction matters because it undercuts the alarmist framing that sometimes accompanies quantum computing coverage. The correct headline is not "no defense exists against the coming quantum threat." It is, less dramatically but more accurately, "a defense has existed in mature form for years, and the current work is deploying it broadly before it becomes urgent." That deployment work has already produced concrete, government backed standards, exactly where the next chapter picks up.
